name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 25 September 1973

clue.text: Rodeo Abbey

blocks.note: surface reading: a cowboy show, nothing to do with monks
setter's reading: at a rodeo the broncos buck, and they do it fast, giving the two halves of a Devon abbey's name

explanation.walkthrough: Buckfast Abbey is a Benedictine monastery in Devon, England, famous for its tonic wine. The clue is just two words; the joke is splitting the name into what a rodeo horse does.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckfast is the name of a working Benedictine monastery in Devon, so it is an example of an abbey.

clue.text: Spell cast on Burlington House by power cuts?

blocks.note: when the power is cut everything goes black
Burlington House in London is home to the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: Someone imagines the blackouts of the 1970s as a curse laid on a London gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: Burlington House, on Piccadilly, holds the Royal Academy, Britain's national art academy. The black piece is placed on top of the art piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Black art means black magic, sorcery, so a spell is an instance of it.

clue.text: One that can ring a hare? '

definitions.text: One that can ring a hare?

blocks.clueFragment: One that can ring a hare?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone or something able to surround and trap a hare
setter's reading: the plant family whose flowers are bells includes the harebell, so it can ring a hare-bell

explanation.walkthrough: The harebell is a small blue wild bellflower, and it belongs to the genus Latin calls 'little bell'. The clue jokes that a bellflower could ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Campanula is the bellflower genus, which includes the harebell, so it is the plant with bells.

clue.text: Something fishy is seen on the last page

blocks.note: a fin belongs to a fish
taken as written

explanation.surface: A suspicious detail spotted at the end of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something fishy' looks like something suspicious; it is literally a part of a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Finis is the Latin word for 'the end', traditionally printed at the close of a book or film.

clue.text: Put in one's place

blocks.note: surface reading: to humble someone, take them down a peg
setter's reading: literally to set something in its position

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means to snub someone; read literally it means to position something, which is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To situate something is to give it a site, placing it in a particular position or location.

clue.text: Thwart the creature

blocks.note: first meaning: to put a stop to a plan, as in to put paid to a rumour
second meaning: 'the creature' (the crayture) is an old Irish and Scots nickname for whisky

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to block an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The creature' reads as an animal, but it is the jocular name for whisky, and whisky from Scotland has a one-word name.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a scheme is to stop it dead, and Scotch is whisky, the drink nicknamed the creature.

clue.text: Slightly humped grass land in Surrey

blocks.note: a camber is the slight convex rise across a road
a ley is land laid down to grass

explanation.surface: A gently rolling meadow somewhere in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: Camberley is a town in Surrey, a county just south-west of London, home of the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: Camberley is a town in the English county of Surrey, so it is a piece of land there.

clue.text: Horatius's father

blocks.note: surface reading: the parent of the Roman hero who held the bridge
setter's reading: in Macaulay's poem the hero prays to the river as 'father', before swimming home across it

explanation.walkthrough: In Macaulay's 'Horatius' the hero cries 'Oh Tiber! father Tiber, To whom the Romans pray' before leaping into the river. The scan's OCR dropped the i from Horatius.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romans called their river Father Tiber, and Horatius addresses it with that title in Macaulay's poem.

clue.text: Island saint of the bard's dream

blocks.note: first meaning: Saint ..., the South Atlantic island where Napoleon died in exile
second meaning: one of the four young lovers in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: A holy woman from an island who appears in one of Shakespeare's plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bard' is Shakespeare, and 'dream' points to A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: St Helena is a remote British island named after a saint, and Helena loves Demetrius in Shakespeare's comedy.

clue.text: Paul was anti-British

blocks.note: surface reading: points first to Paul Revere, who rode to warn of British troops in America
setter's reading: another Paul led the Transvaal against Britain in the Boer War

explanation.walkthrough: Paul Revere is the obvious anti-British Paul but is too short and crosses wrongly; the other is the Boer president of the Transvaal.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Kruger was president of the South African Republic and led Boer resistance to Britain in the Boer War.

clue.text: A carpet to give a religious iconoclast ideas?

blocks.clueFragment: A carpet to give a religious iconoclast ideas?
blocks.note: surface reading: a rug whose pattern might inspire someone who smashes church images
setter's reading: an iconoclast's idea would be to take an axe to a minster, a great church; say those two words together and you have a type of carpet

explanation.walkthrough: An Axminster is a machine-woven carpet named after the Devon town where it was first made; read as 'axe minster' it is exactly what an image-breaker would like to do.
explanation.definitionFit: Axminster is a well-known kind of pile carpet, originally woven in the town of that name in Devon.

clue.text: My beautiful one before the French

definitions.text: My beautiful one before the French

blocks.clueFragment: My beautiful one before the French
blocks.note: surface reading: a lover's endearment, set down ahead of something French
setter's reading: a French endearment meaning 'my beauty' is the traditional source of a girl's name, which came first, before the French

explanation.walkthrough: The name is said to come from the French endearment (or from Amabel), so 'my beautiful one' turned into a name; 'before the French' hints that the name grew out of the French phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Mabel is a woman's name popularly derived from the French endearment for a beloved, my beautiful one.

clue.text: Chips off hill-crests

blocks.note: first meaning: to knap is to chip flint into shape, so this is a verb
second meaning: a knap is a dialect word for the crest of a hill, so this is a plural noun

explanation.surface: Pieces broken off the tops of hills.
explanation.definitionFit: Knapping is the flint-worker's term for chipping stone, and a knap is also an old word for a hilltop.

clue.text: Structural support for fish club

blocks.note: to angle is to fish with rod and line
an iron is a kind of golf club

explanation.surface: A sturdy frame being put up to hold an angling society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish club' looks like an angling society; it is two separate pieces, a verb and a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: An angle iron is an L-shaped metal bar used to brace and strengthen frames in building.

clue.text: Libertine without cash for the daily round

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of outside: one word stands around the other

blocks.note: a roué is a debauched man
tin is old slang for money

explanation.surface: A rake who is broke going about his everyday business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without cash' looks like it means having no money; here 'without' means outside, so the libertine wraps around the cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A routine is the regular set of tasks done each day, the same as one's daily round.

clue.text: Magnum for his nibs?

blocks.note: surface reading: a large bottle of champagne for a self-important person, 'his nibs'
setter's reading: nibs are pen points, and the vessel they are dipped in holds writing fluid

explanation.walkthrough: 'His nibs' is British slang for a pompous person, and a magnum is a double-size wine bottle; read literally, the nibs belong to a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: An ink bottle is the container that supplies ink to the nibs of dip pens.

clue.text: "I know not where is that Promethean heat That can thy light —" (Othello)

definitions.text: "I know not where is that Promethean heat That can thy light —" (Othello)

blocks.clueFragment: "I know not where is that Promethean heat That can thy light —"
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of Shakespeare with its last word missing
setter's reading: Othello says this over the sleeping Desdemona, comparing her life to a candle he cannot light again once put out; the missing verb means to rekindle

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Othello, Act 5 Scene 2: 'I know not where is that Promethean heat / That can thy light relume.'
explanation.definitionFit: Relume is an old word meaning to light again or rekindle, which is what the quotation needs.

clue.text: One David's stepfather half-murdered by another's missile

indicators.note: 'half' keeps only one of the two equal parts of the word that follows, here the front

blocks.note: taken as written before it is cut
the other David, the biblical shepherd boy, killed Goliath with a stone from his sling

explanation.surface: A tale of a stepfather nearly killed by a projectile thrown by someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: The first David is Dickens's David Copperfield, whose cruel stepfather is Mr Murdstone; the second is King David.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Murdstone marries David Copperfield's widowed mother in Dickens's novel, becoming the boy's harsh stepfather.

clue.text: Poet set to work again as he drove back

blocks.note: first meaning, a pun: a poet put back to writing verse has been ...
second meaning: a driver who drove backwards put the car into reverse

explanation.surface: A poet goes back to his job while driving home.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half splits the word as re + versed, verse being the poet's work.
explanation.definitionFit: To have reversed a car is to have driven it backwards, so the past tense fits drove back.

clue.text: Inquisitive one whom 28 has his eye on

blocks.note: first meaning: a Nosy ... is a busybody, so the surname alone stands for a prying person
second meaning: 28 across is a warden, and a traffic warden watches the person who parks a car

explanation.surface: A nosy person being kept under watch by an official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nosy Parker' is a common English phrase for a busybody. A traffic warden is the official who issues parking tickets.
explanation.definitionFit: Parker is short for Nosy Parker, a meddler, and is also simply one who parks a vehicle.

clue.text: One horn's crumbled of those that may have two

indicators.note: something crumbled has broken into pieces, which can be put back together differently

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A beast with two horns has had one broken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two' refers back to the horns: some species have one horn and others two.
explanation.definitionFit: African rhinoceroses have two horns on the snout, so rhinos are animals that may have two.

clue.text: Flourishing supplier of famous headwear

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; it stands for flourishing through the phrase 'flourishing like a green bay tree'

blocks.note: first meaning: Psalm 37 speaks of the wicked 'spreading himself like a green ...', and the phrase means thriving
second meaning: the leaves of the laurel gave the victor's wreath worn by Roman heroes and poets

explanation.walkthrough: 'Supplier of famous headwear' sounds like a milliner; the headwear is the laurel crown, made from bay leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The bay laurel is the evergreen whose leaves made victors' crowns, and it is proverbial for thriving growth.

clue.text: Post-graduate point for charging for the remainder

indicators.note: 'post' means after, so the next piece follows the graduate's letters

blocks.note: a Bachelor of Arts is a graduate
a knight charges with the point of his lance

explanation.surface: A university course with fees charged for the rest of the term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post-graduate' looks like advanced study; it is an instruction to put something after a graduate's degree letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The balance is what is left over, as in the balance owed or the balance of the day.

clue.text: School of adversity?

blocks.note: surface reading: the hard school of life, where one learns from misfortune
setter's reading: a famous English private school whose name, as a verb, means to distress

explanation.walkthrough: Harrow is a famous English boarding school near London; to harrow someone is to torment them, hence 'harrowing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrow is a well-known English school, and its name as a verb means to cause great distress.

clue.text: Just too deliciously pagan for the Saint

blocks.note: first meaning: ambrosia was the food of the Greek gods, so something tasting divine in a heathen way
second meaning: read as an adjective belonging to Saint Ambrose, the fourth-century bishop of Milan

explanation.surface: A gushing verdict that something is too heathen and delightful for a holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a joke: an adjective formed from St Ambrose's name looks just like the word for divinely delicious.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrosial means exquisitely delicious, like the food of the classical gods, who were pagan deities.

clue.text: Package operator to Hay?

blocks.note: surface reading: a holiday tour firm running trips to Hay, the Welsh border book town
setter's reading: a farm machine that packs hay into bundles

explanation.walkthrough: The capital H dresses hay up as Hay-on-Wye, the town on the Wales–England border; the 'package' is a bundle of hay.
explanation.definitionFit: A baler is the machine that compresses hay or straw into tied bundles called bales.

clue.text: Exclusive system in EEC as terms are named

indicators.note: 'in' says the answer sits inside the run of words that follows, spanning their boundaries

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Britain had just joined the Common Market, and its terms of entry looked like a closed club.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan's OCR reads 'EFC is'; the word was EEC, the European Economic Community Britain joined in 1973, and the letters run on from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste system divides society into hereditary classes that exclude outsiders, so it is an exclusive system.

clue.text: Hippy

blocks.note: surface reading: a long-haired flower child of the sixties
setter's reading: read as 'of the hip', the anatomical adjective formed from the Latin for hip

explanation.walkthrough: A one-word pun: the anatomical adjective comes from Latin coxa, hip.
explanation.definitionFit: Coxal is the anatomical adjective meaning relating to the hip or hip joint.

clue.text: Doorkeeper returned to 16, which he did

definitions.note: refers to 16 across, a past-tense sense: lit again

indicators.note: something returned comes back the way it went, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: in Freemasonry the tiler guards the door of the lodge

explanation.surface: A doorman came back to relight the lamp, as he duly did.
explanation.walkthrough: The Masonic tiler is the lodge's doorkeeper. 16 across is RELUME, light again, and the reversed word is its past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Relit is the past tense of relight, the plain English for relume, to kindle again.

clue.text: Possible boon to Sioux maybe? Just the opposite!

definitions.note: the opposite of a boon, taken as an adjective: hateful

indicators.note: 'possible' offers one arrangement among many that the letters could take

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something that might be a gift to a Plains tribe turns out to be quite the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the end of the clue: the opposite of a boon is something offensive. The Sioux are a Native American people of the Great Plains.
explanation.definitionFit: Obnoxious means highly unpleasant or offensive, the reverse of a welcome favour or blessing.

clue.text: Officer on the watch from dug-out?

definitions.text: Officer on the watch from dug-out?

blocks.clueFragment: Officer on the watch from dug-out?
blocks.note: surface reading: a soldier or sailor keeping lookout from a trench shelter
setter's reading: a wartime air-raid official kept watch from a shelter, and the same title goes on game reserves and traffic duty

explanation.walkthrough: In the Second World War, ARP (Air Raid Precautions) officials patrolled during blackouts and worked from shelters; their title is also that of a prison guard or park keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A warden is an official whose job is watching over a place or people, such as an air-raid patrol officer.

clue.text: Migraine cured — and here is spring!

blocks.note: cured means healthy again
a migraine is a bad head, a severe headache

explanation.surface: A headache sufferer, finally better, cheers the arrival of the new season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season; it is a source of water. A head made better reads as the two pieces in reverse order.
explanation.definitionFit: A wellhead is the source of a spring or stream, the point where the water rises from the ground.
